messages.subject: low acceptance rate of INLA MCMC method
messages.subject_clean: low acceptance rate of INLA MCMC method
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I try to use the INLA MCMC method in the Bym example of volume 1. I
set inla.arg = "-m mcmc -N 500 -T 10 -S 1" as in
demo("Tokyo-compare"). But the acceptance rate is very low (around
0.03) and decreasing. I tried several -S values from 0.5 to 20 but the acceptance rate was still very low.

Is there a way to improve the acceptance rate?

The R code is below.

Thanks for helpful comments.
Best,

Florian

-------------------------------------------------------------------------

rm(list=ls())
require(INLA)
data(Oral)
g <- system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")
Oral.inla <- cbind(Oral,region.struct=Oral$region)

formula <- Y ~ -1 +
  f(region.struct,model="besag",graph=g,hyper=list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.5), initial=log(15)))) +
  f(region,model="iid",hyper=list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.01), initial=log(222))))

## INLA MCMC
## similar to demo("Tokyo-compare")
im.out <- inla(formula,family="poisson",data=Oral.inla,E=E,
  working.directory =  tempfile(), keep=TRUE, inla.arg = "-m mcmc -N 500 -T 10 -S 1", verbose=TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
This is a general question about space time models. I have used BUGS to do these models in the past, following the specifications of Knorr-Held (Type1 -- Type 4 Space-Time interactions), and see the example in the case studies of Blangiardo-et-al-2012, that uses the Type 1 (unstructured S-T interaction) but was wondering if anyone has tried the other types of interaction (separate time by space, separate space by time and full space-time interaction). I think that the key is using an A matrix specification from the Kroneker products of the space and time dependence matrices, but I don't know how to go about doing this.
Any advice would be most welcome
Corey

The intended way of doing that with inla.spde.make.A() is to define a
mapping between continuous space/time and the discrete model
representation using a "1d mesh".

inla.spde.make.A(...,

In older versions, you need

    group=time,
    group.mesh=inla.mesh.1d(time),
    group.method="nearest")

Finn

On 17 maj 2013, at 21:34, ximing <siem...@gmail.com> wrote:
> In the R-INLA package, we have the model options of  random walk of order 1 and 2 for the latent states;
> can we also fit a random walk model with drift ?   Thanks.

The easiest method is to reparameterise the processes.  The solutions to
  x'(t) = mu + dB(t)
can be written as
  x(t) = mu * t + z(t)
where z(t) is the RW from
  z'(t) = dB(t)
and similarly for second order models.

So a RW(1) with drift according to this definition is equivalent to a non drift RW plus a linear effect of time, which can be simply added as an ordinary covariate, and mu estimated as a "fixed effect".
This also gives the posteriors for x(t) in the linear predictor.

If you had some other model in mind, please specify.

Finn

messages.subject: Obtain summary of posterior predictive distribution
messages.subject_clean: Obtain summary of posterior predictive distribution
messages.body_plain:
When response values are set to NA and control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE), the values in summary.fitted.values correspond to posterior summaries of the linear predictor. However, we are interested in summaries of the posterior predictive distribution, that is, we would like summaries of predicted values of the response not the predicted value of the linear predictor.

To obtain posterior summaries of predicted values, I specify the overall error term as an "iid" random effect and fixed the precision of the gaussian family to be extremely large, control.family=list(initial=12,fixed=TRUE). Does this seem reasonable? A working example is described below.

Consider the following working example based on the attached dataset and r-code(commented). The data comes from a split-plot experiment with 2 whole-plot factors (one with 2 levels and one with 6 levels), and one split-plot factor (with 3 levels). There were 4 replicates at each of the 12 combinations of the whole plot factors. A model for the data can be written as

Y_{ijkl} =  \alpha_ i + \beta_ j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \eta_{ l(ij)}+\gamma_k +(\alpha\gamma)_{ ik} + (\beta\gamma) _{jk} + (\alpha\beta\gamma)_{ijk} + \epsilon_l(ijk)

where i indexes whole-plot factor 1, j indexes whole-plot factor 2, k indexes the split plot factor and l indexes replicate. We assume \eta_{ l(ij)} - the whole plot error term - is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance $\sigma^2_{\eta}$ and the split-plot error term $\epsilon_l(ijk)$ is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance $\sigma^2_{\epsilon}$.

The data set has the following columns - ID, Response, repXwp1wp2, wp1, sp, wp2.

The attached r-code reads in the data, creates a data frame for predicting response at each of the 36 combinations if wp1, sp, wp2 and merges the two data frames. Then the model with $\epsilon$ specified as an "iid" effect is fit and posterior summaries are obtained. Finally, the model with $\epsilon$ assumed to be the family error term is fit and posterior summaries are obtained. The results are plotted for both models in 3X2 arrays in posteriorpred.pdf and posteriorpredlinpred.pdf. Notice the width of the credible intervals is larger for the plots in posteriorpred.pdf.

Thanks,

yes you are correct. I interpret your post as a comment only, so I
follow up with my comment on it. Yes, it's is a cool trick.

Here are two models:

A. y ~ 1 + x with family="gaussian"

B. y ~ 1 + x + f(idx,model="iid"), with idx=1:n, family="gaussian" with
a fixed high precision.

the difference, is that the linear.predictor in A is 1+x, while in B its
1+x+f(idx) which is the *the observed data* if y[idx[i]] and the
predictive distribution for a new observation, if y[idx[i]]=NA. so what
you need to do is to replicate the model.

This simple(r) example, demonstrate this.

n = 100
x = rnorm(n)
y = 1 + x + rnorm(n, sd=0.1)

r = inla(y ~ 1 + x,
        data = data.frame(y, x),
        control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE),
        control.family = list(
                hyper = list(prec = list(param=c(1, 0.01)))))

xx = c(x, x)
yy = c(y, rep(NA, n))
ii = c(1:n, 1:n)
rr = inla(yy ~ 1 + xx +
        f(ii, model="iid", hyper = list(prec = list(param=c(1,
0.01)))),
        data = data.frame(yy, xx),
        control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial=20,
fixed=TRUE))),
        control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE))

## this should be almost zero
r$summary.fixed-rr$summary.fixed

## plot of the i'th observation with the predictive distribution as

messages.body_plain:
Dear R-inla discussion group,
I am using rw2d models for spatial data of coastal seabird densities. Until now, I fitted models for each survey (n=3, all in the same area) separately. However, although birds may move along the coast, they are generally located at certain water depths. Therefore, I'd like to use this shared information between surveys - ultimately to estimate gaps in less complete surveys.

I tried this:

   ncol = length(unique(x))
   nrow = length(unique(y))
   n = ncol * nrow
   node1 = c(1:n, rep(NA,2*n))
   node2 = c(rep(NA,n), 1:n, rep(NA,n))
   node3 = c(rep(NA,2*n), 1:n)               # nodes for the rw2d model; each set of nodes corresponding to a survey, others set to NA
   ftrip = factor(c(1:3), each=n)              # to get an intercept for each survey

   formula = count ~ depth + f(node1, model="rw2d", ncol=ncol, nrow=nrow) +  f(node2, model="rw2d", ncol=ncol, nrow=nrow) +  f(node3, model="rw2d", ncol=ncol, nrow=nrow) + ftrip -1

   result = inla(formula, data=data, family="nbinomial", offset=offsetter)

I'd like to have your opinion about whether this is a good idea in general and/or if there are better ways of doing this.

Rob

messages.body_plain:
On 23/05/13 21:22, Rob van Bemmelen wrote:
> I am using rw2d models for spatial data of coastal seabird densities.

> generally located at certain water depths. Therefore, I'd like to use

Yes, the essence of this seems good.  If you also want also want to
borrow strength by assuming that all three surveys should have the same
precision parameter for the rw2d effect, you can use just a single f(),
and specify that there are three independent replications of the same model:

ncol = length(unique(x))
nrow = length(unique(y))
n = ncol * nrow

node = rep(1:n, times=3) ## Each node is used once per survey
repl = rep(1:3, each=n) ## Three surveys, each with n nodes

ftrip = factor(c(1:3), each=n) # to get an intercept for each survey

formula = count ~ depth + f(node, model="rw2d", ncol=ncol, nrow=nrow,
replicate=repl) + ftrip -1

/Finn
